summary: Alberta votes Monday on whether to start a path toward leaving Canada, and Carney is rallying there. Health ministers say a one-year federal funding extension is not enough.
body: The main Canadian story this week is in Alberta. On Monday, Oct. 19, Albertans vote on 10 referendum questions. Question 10 asks whether Alberta should stay a province of Canada or whether the provincial government should start the legal process toward a binding vote on separating [^3]. Turnout is running high: Elections Alberta said 174,532 people voted on the first of five advance polling days, more than the daily average in the 2023 provincial election [^4]. A Leger online poll from early October found 70% would choose to remain and 22% would choose to start the separation process [^5].

Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke Thursday night at a 'Forever Canadian' rally in Calgary. His office put the crowd at about 5,000 [^2]. He said Alberta's frustrations are real, called a vote against Canada a risky bluff, and asked for 'a decisive result on Monday' [^1][^2]. He also said people outside Canada want to 'break us so they can own us,' without naming anyone [^2]. Premier Danielle Smith wants a 'yes' on the other nine questions, which cover immigration and the Constitution, as a message to Ottawa; critics call some of them anti-immigrant [^2]. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was set to speak in Calgary on Friday in support of unity [^1].

On health care, Ottawa is extending $1.2 billion in funding for mental health, addictions and home care by one year [^6]. Provincial health ministers met in Winnipeg and said that is only a first step. They want the Canada Health Transfer, the main federal health payment to provinces, to grow at least 5% a year instead of dropping to 3% in 2028. Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones said the extension adds no new programs and does not give long-term certainty [^6].

Closer to home, the Supreme Court of Canada heard a challenge to the Ontario law that cleared the way for the Ontario Place redevelopment. A coalition argues the law wrongly blocks court review; Ontario says it does not make the site 'a lawless zone.' A ruling may not come until 2027 [^7]. Otherwise it was a fairly quiet few days for Ontario politics and economic data.
differences: Health funding: Ottawa says the one-year extension gives stability while it works to strengthen health care, while provincial ministers say it only delays a coming funding shortfall and want faster transfer growth [^6]. Alberta: Smith frames the other nine questions as a message about provincial autonomy; critics call some of them anti-immigrant [^2].
